title: Probability, Crosses and the Chi-Square Test

generated.pipeline: extract → Opus draft → Sonnet accuracy gate → Sonnet fixes

cards.front: For independent events, the chance that both happen is the {{c1::product}} of their chances (the product rule).
cards.back: P(X and Y) = P(X) × P(Y)
cards.quote: For independent events, the chance of both is the product (the product rule):
cards.section: Two rules: and means multiply, or means add

cards.front: For mutually exclusive events, the chance that either happens is the {{c1::sum}} of their chances (the sum rule).
cards.back: P(X or Y) = P(X) + P(Y). Mutually exclusive means they cannot both happen.
cards.quote: Two events are mutually exclusive when they cannot both happen; the chance of either is then the sum (the sum rule):
cards.section: Two rules: and means multiply, or means add

cards.front: In the cross Aa × Aa, why is the chance of an Aa offspring 1/2 rather than 1/4?
cards.back: Aa arises in two mutually exclusive ways: A from the egg and a from the sperm, or the reverse. Each is 1/2 × 1/2 = 1/4, and the sum rule adds them: 1/2.
cards.quote: It is Aa in two exclusive ways (A from the egg and a from the sperm, or the reverse): 1/4 + 1/4 = 1/2.
cards.section: Two rules: and means multiply, or means add

cards.front: In the cross Aa × Aa with complete dominance, what fraction of offspring shows the dominant phenotype (A_)?
cards.back: 3/4. A_ is AA or Aa, which are mutually exclusive: 1/4 + 1/2 = 3/4.
cards.quote: It shows the dominant phenotype, written A_ (the blank stands for either allele), if it is AA or Aa: 1/4 + 1/2 = 3/4.
cards.section: Two rules: and means multiply, or means add

cards.front: Why may single-gene chances be multiplied for genes on different chromosomes?
cards.back: They assort independently, because each pair of chromosomes lines up in meiosis without regard to the others. Independence is the condition the product rule needs.
cards.quote: Genes on different chromosomes assort independently, because each pair of chromosomes lines up in meiosis without regard to the others.
cards.section: Two rules: and means multiply, or means add

cards.front: Why can single-gene chances not simply be multiplied for two genes close together on one chromosome, when they can almost be multiplied for genes far apart on it?
cards.back: Close genes tend to be inherited together, so they are not independent. Far-apart genes behave almost as if unlinked, because crossing over reshuffles them in close to half of the gametes.
cards.quote: Genes close together on one chromosome tend to be inherited together, so their single-gene chances can no longer simply be multiplied
cards.section: Two rules: and means multiply, or means add

cards.front: What is the branch (forked-line) method for a cross of several unlinked genes?
cards.back: Treat each gene as its own small cross: at each locus branch into dominant (3/4) or recessive (1/4) phenotype. A path's probability is the product along it.
cards.quote: Treat each gene as its own small cross: at each locus, branch into the dominant phenotype (3/4) or the recessive one (1/4).
cards.section: Many genes at once: multiply along the branches

cards.front: In the cross AaBbCc × AaBbCc (three unlinked genes, complete dominance, no selection), what fraction of offspring is A_ bb C_?
cards.section: Many genes at once: multiply along the branches

cards.front: In AaBbCc × AaBbCc (three unlinked genes, complete dominance), is an offspring dominant for exactly two of the three traits more, less or equally likely than one dominant for all three?
cards.back: Equally likely, 27/64 each. All three dominant is one path, (3/4)^3. Each exactly-two path is only 9/64, but there are three of them (any trait can be the recessive one), and exclusive paths add.
cards.why: The factor of three, counting which trait is recessive, is the one most people forget.
cards.quote: But there are three such paths, one for each trait that could be the recessive one, and that factor of three is the one most people forget.
cards.section: Many genes at once: multiply along the branches

cards.front: In AaBbCc × AaBbCc (three unlinked genes, complete dominance), what fraction of offspring is dominant for exactly one of the three traits?
cards.back: 9/64. Each such path has one 3/4 and two 1/4 factors: 3/4 × 1/4 × 1/4 = 3/64. Three exclusive paths (the dominant trait can be A, B or C): 3 × 3/64 = 9/64.
cards.why: Check: 27/64 + 27/64 + 9/64 + 1/64 = 64/64, so no path was missed.
cards.quote: exactly one, 9/64 (three paths of 3/64 each); and none, 1/64.
cards.section: Counting all eight paths

cards.front: Two carrier parents (Aa) have a first child who is aa. Is the chance their second child is aa now still 1/4?
cards.back: Yes, still 1/4. Each child is an independent draw from the same parents; the first changes nothing for the second.
cards.why: Believing the family has used up its affected child is the gambler's fallacy.
cards.quote: Believing that the family has "used up" its affected child is the gambler's fallacy; segregation has no memory.
cards.section: Families: the binomial counts the birth orders

cards.front: Complete {{c1::penetrance}} means every aa child shows the trait.
cards.back: This is an assumption of the exercise, not a general fact about genotypes.
cards.quote: Assume complete penetrance (every aa child shows the trait) and that each child is an independent event with probability 1/4.
cards.section: Families: the binomial counts the birth orders

cards.front: The binomial probability of k affected children out of n combines which two parts?
cards.back: The chance of one particular birth order, p^k (1 − p)^(n − k), multiplied by the number of orders, n! / (k! (n − k)!).
cards.why: The number of orders is the factor most often forgotten.
cards.quote: Step 1 had two parts: the chance of one particular order, then the number of orders, the factor most often forgotten.
cards.section: Families: the binomial counts the birth orders

cards.front: Two carrier parents (Aa) have four children. Assuming complete penetrance and independent births, what is the chance that exactly one child is aa?
cards.back: One order: 1/4 × (3/4)^3 = 27/256. The affected child can be any of four, so 4 × 27/256 = 108/256 = 27/64, about 0.42.
cards.section: Families: the binomial counts the birth orders

cards.front: Two carrier parents (Aa) have four children. What is the chance that exactly two are aa?
cards.section: Families: the binomial counts the birth orders

cards.front: Two carrier parents (Aa) have four children. What is the chance that at least one is aa, and what is the quickest route?
cards.back: Use the complement. P(none) = (3/4)^4 = 81/256, so P(at least one) = 1 − 81/256 = 175/256, about 0.68.
cards.why: "At least one" is everything except "none", which is a single term.
cards.quote: Use the complement: "at least one" is everything except "none".
cards.section: Families: the binomial counts the birth orders

cards.front: Among 256 families of four children from two carrier (Aa) parents, how many are expected to have exactly three aa children?
cards.why: Expected only; observed numbers would scatter around it.
cards.quote: Among 256 real families, 81, 108, 54, 12 and 1 are only the expected numbers with 0 to 4 affected; the observed numbers would scatter.
cards.section: Families: the binomial counts the birth orders

cards.front: Two carrier parents with four children expect one aa child on average. Why is that not what most families get?
cards.back: The mean is 4 × 1/4 = 1, but the chance of exactly one is only about 42% (108/256), and of none about 32% (81/256). A probability predicts a spread, not one count.
cards.quote: On average a family of four has one affected child (4 × 1/4 = 1), but no family is promised the average
cards.section: Families: the binomial counts the birth orders

cards.front: Mendel's 556 dihybrid seeds (315, 108, 101, 32) match none of the 9:3:3:1 expected counts. Why is an exact match impossible here?
cards.back: The expected counts (312.75, 104.25, 104.25, 34.75) are fractions of a seed. The real question is whether the misses are ordinary chance scatter.
cards.quote: None of his counts matches. It could not: the expected counts are fractions of a seed.

cards.front: How is the chi-square statistic computed from observed and expected counts?
cards.back: For each class, (observed − expected)² / expected; then sum over all classes.
cards.why: Dividing by the expected count judges each miss against the scatter normal for that class.
cards.quote: So a fair score judges each miss against the scatter in its own class.
cards.section: Is the deviation chance? The chi-square test

cards.front: Coin A: 10 tosses, 6 heads. Coin B: 100 tosses, 60 heads. Compute chi-square against 50:50 for each. Which result is more surprising?
cards.back: B: (60 − 50)²/50 + (40 − 50)²/50 = 4. A: (6 − 5)²/5 + (4 − 5)²/5 = 0.4. Same proportions, a tenth of the score; B is more surprising.
cards.why: Chance moves a count by an amount that grows with the count, but more slowly than the count.
cards.quote: Same proportions, a tenth of the score, because a small sample strays easily by chance.
cards.section: Is the deviation chance? The chi-square test

cards.front: If the hypothesized ratio holds, chi-square lands on average at its {{c1::degrees of freedom}}.
cards.back: Well above that, chance becomes a poor explanation.
cards.quote: If the ratio holds, chi-square lands on average at its degrees of freedom; well above that, chance becomes a poor explanation.
cards.section: Is the deviation chance? The chi-square test

cards.front: Why does a chi-square test of four phenotype classes against a ratio fixed in advance have 3 degrees of freedom, not 4?
cards.back: The classes share one total: once three counts and the total are known, the fourth is set. Only three misses are free: df = 4 − 1.
cards.quote: The ratio was fixed in advance, but the four classes share one total: once three counts and the total are known, the fourth is set.
cards.section: Is the deviation chance? The chi-square test

cards.front: A dihybrid F2 of 160 plants gives 98, 28, 26 and 8 in the four phenotype classes. Test against 9:3:3:1 (critical value 7.81 at 0.05 with 3 df).
cards.quote: A dihybrid F2 of 160 plants gives 98, 28, 26 and 8 in the four phenotype classes.
cards.section: Is the deviation chance? The chi-square test

cards.front: The critical value is the chi-square score that only {{c1::5%}} of chance results exceed; with 3 df it is 7.81.
cards.back: A score above it rejects the ratio at the 0.05 level.
cards.quote: The critical value is the score that only 5% of chance results exceed; with 3 df it is 7.81 (from a chi-square table or software).
cards.section: Is the deviation chance? The chi-square test

cards.front: Why must a chi-square test use counts, never percentages or ratios?
cards.back: The size of the sample is what makes a miss surprising. Percentages erase sample size, so the same split scores the same at any n.
cards.quote: Use counts, never percentages or ratios, because the size of the sample is what makes a miss surprising.
cards.section: Is the deviation chance? The chi-square test

cards.front: What expected-count condition keeps a chi-square test honest, and what should replace it when the condition fails?
cards.back: About five or more expected in every class. Below that the chi-square approximation becomes poor; an exact test or a simulation of the cross does better.
cards.quote: And keep the expected count at about five or more in every class.
cards.section: Is the deviation chance? The chi-square test

cards.front: A p-value is the probability of getting data {{c1::at least this far from expectation}} if the hypothesis and every other assumption of the model were true.
cards.back: It is not the probability that the hypothesis is true.
cards.quote: A p-value is the probability of getting data at least this far from expectation if the hypothesis and every other assumption of the model were true.
cards.section: What a p-value does and does not tell you

cards.front: A chi-square test gives p > 0.05. Does that prove the hypothesized ratio?
cards.back: No. You fail to reject it. Other models may fit the same counts as well.
cards.quote: So p > 0.05 does not prove the hypothesis: it means you fail to reject it.
cards.section: What a p-value does and does not tell you

cards.front: A dihybrid F2 gives a large chi-square against 9:3:3:1 and p far below 0.05. A student concludes the genes are linked. Is that justified?
cards.back: No. The test rejects the model but does not say which assumption failed: linkage, a lethal genotype or misscored plants can all inflate chi-square.
cards.quote: A small p-value does not tell you which assumption failed, either: linkage, a lethal genotype and misscored plants can all inflate chi-square.
cards.section: What a p-value does and does not tell you

cards.front: An F2 tested against 9:3:3:1 gives chi-square 0.05 with 3 df, an almost perfect match. Should that reassure you?
cards.back: Not entirely. With 3 df fewer than 1 chance result in 300 lands that close. One can be luck, but repeated scores far below the df suggest asking how the counts were gathered and scored.
cards.why: The lower tail flags a fit too close, as the upper tail flags one too far.
cards.quote: The lower tail of the distribution, the scores near zero, flags a fit that is too close, as the upper tail flags one that is too far.
cards.section: What a p-value does and does not tell you

cards.front: Two true-breeding white-flowered lines give an all-purple F1. The F2 of 160 has 96 purple and 64 white. Test 3:1 and 9:7 (critical value 3.84 at 0.05, 1 df).
cards.back: 3:1: expected 120 and 40; chi-square = 4.8 + 14.4 = 19.2, rejected. 9:7: expected 90 and 70; chi-square = 0.40 + 0.51 = 0.91, p about 0.34, not rejected.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: An F2 of 96 purple and 64 white fits 9:7 well. Why does that fit alone not establish the two-gene model, and what does 9:7 offer that a fit does not?
cards.back: A 5:3 ratio fits these counts too (chi-square about 0.43), and no one proposes it. 9:7 adds a mechanism, two genes each needed for purple, which further crosses can test.
cards.quote: A good fit does not establish the model: a 5:3 ratio (100:60) fits these counts too, with chi-square about 0.43, and no one is proposing it.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: Two true-breeding white-flowered lines are crossed and the F1 is all purple. In the simple model of recessive loss-of-function mutations, what does this suggest?
cards.back: The lines are mutant in different genes. Two lines mutant in the same gene would give a white F1, so an all-purple F1 is the classic sign of two genes.
cards.why: Exceptions such as intragenic complementation exist.
cards.quote: In the simple model, where each white line carries a fully penetrant recessive loss-of-function mutation, two lines mutant in the same gene would give a white F1.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: To decide whether white flowers in an F2 come from one gene or two genes each needed for purple, which cross separates the models, and which does not?
cards.back: Cross F2 white plants with each other in many pairs: one gene predicts only white; two genes predict some pairs (aa × bb types) giving purple. Backcrossing F1 to a white parent fails: both models predict about 1 purple : 1 white.
cards.quote: Under two genes, some pairs (one carrying aa, the other bb, each with the other gene's dominant allele) give purple offspring.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: Why does chi-square average k − 1 when a k-class ratio holds?
cards.back: Each class adds on average 1 − p, where p is that class's predicted probability. The p's sum to 1, so the averages sum to k − 1, at any sample size.
cards.quote: If the ratio holds, each class adds on average 1 − p to chi-square, where p is that class's predicted probability.
cards.section: Why the chance pile balances at the degrees of freedom

cards.front: How many degrees of freedom has a goodness-of-fit test against four classes, versus a 2 × 2 test of whether two traits are associated?
cards.back: Goodness of fit, four classes: 3 df. 2 × 2 association test: 1 df.
cards.quote: a goodness-of-fit test against four classes has 3 df, while a 2 × 2 test of whether two traits are associated has 1 df.
cards.section: Degrees of freedom when you estimate from the data

cards.front: A student tests a 16-plant dihybrid F2 against 9:3:3:1 with the usual 7.81 cutoff. What is wrong, and how does the test misbehave?
cards.back: The smallest expected count is 1, below about five, so the chi-square approximation is poor. In a simulation, a true 9:3:3:1 was rejected 4.1% of the time, not 5%. Use an exact test or a simulation.
cards.quote: In a simulation of 16-plant F2s, where the smallest expected count is 1, a true 9:3:3:1 was rejected 4.1% of the time, not 5%.
cards.section: Small expected counts

cards.front: An F2 of 400 plants gives 280 dominant and 120 recessive, tested against 3:1 (critical value 3.84, 1 df). Compare the result using counts with the result using percentages (70, 30 vs 75, 25).
cards.back: Counts: expected 300 and 100; chi-square = 400/300 + 400/100 = 1.33 + 4 = 5.33, so 3:1 is rejected. Percentages: 25/75 + 25/25 = 1.33, wrongly not rejected.
cards.why: Rests on the counts rule: sample size is what makes a miss surprising.
cards.quote: Chance moves a count by an amount that grows with the count, but more slowly than the count.
cards.section: Is the deviation chance? The chi-square test
